summary: A 1974 note sharing experience from implementing the Reconnection Protocol in the RSEXEC system, which let users on the ARPANET keep working across sites. It is a report of lessons learned.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 671 describes a Telnet procedure for joining two connected processes directly so an intermediary can leave the communication path. It reports implementation issues with simultaneous requests, timing and error recovery.

questions: what does the telnet reconnection protocol do
subtitle: Implementation notes for using Telnet reconnection to remove an intermediary.

tldr.problem: When an initiating process connects two correspondent processes, it remains in their communication path unless a reconnection procedure can create a direct connection.
tldr.mechanism: The modified Telnet option asks both correspondents to agree, assigns one to listen and one to connect, exchanges host and socket parameters, and then lets the initiator close its connections.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports experimental RSEXEC/TENEX implementation details, including race handling, synchronization and error-recovery concerns.

today: RFC 671 documents a modified experimental Telnet reconnection option and implementation experience with RSEXEC on TENEX.

sections.title: Why Reconnect Two Processes
sections.content: The RFC reports on a modified experimental Telnet reconnection option in RSEXEC. Reconnection changes a setup in which an initiating process has connections to two correspondent processes into a direct connection between the correspondents. Once it succeeds, the initiator is no longer in their communication path.
sections.plainLanguage: An intermediary can connect two other processes, then arrange a direct connection between them. The intermediary can close its connections after the new path is established.

sections.title: Negotiating and Establishing the New Path
sections.content:
The initiator sends IAC DO RECONNECT over each of its two send connections and waits for both correspondents to accept with IAC WILL RECONNECT. If both accept, the initiator chooses one as passive, to listen, and the other as active, to send connection requests. It sends the passive process the destination host and four bytes naming the active process's send socket.

After the passive side accepts the parameters and starts listening, the initiator supplies the same connection information to the active side. When it accepts, the active process sends the requests for the new connections, and the initiator can close its own connections. Rejections require the initiator to cancel the other request or restore communication where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must agree before the intermediary arranges the direct path. One side listens, the other connects, and the intermediary closes its links after both sides confirm.

sections.title: Races, Timing and Recovery
sections.content:
If both ends request reconnection at once, they compare a value formed from host address and receive socket number. The end with the higher value takes precedence; the other request must wait or be retried after the first attempt completes or is aborted.

The implementation notes also warn about timing and system delays: the listener must be ready before connection requests arrive, and failed attempts may need to be retried. Both send and receive connections should be established in parallel to avoid deadlock. The RFC discusses TENEX limitations around buffering, option negotiation, timeouts and multiple processes sharing a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides try to reconnect at once, their host and socket numbers determine which request goes first. The implementation must also handle delays, retries and the need to establish both directions of the new connection.

sections.title: The TENEX and RSEXEC Experiment
sections.content:
The experiment modeled a TIP user using TIPSER/RSEXEC to connect to a remote host. RSEXEC authenticated the TIP user and offered a TELCONN command; after reconnection, the TIP would be connected directly to the new job and RSEXEC would leave the path. A TENEX process simulated the TIP so the researchers would not need to program the TIP.

The author presents TENEX-specific issues as implementation observations that may have parallels on other systems.
sections.plainLanguage: In the experiment, RSEXEC connected a TIP user to a remote job and then stepped out of the path. A TENEX process simulated the TIP during testing.
